script_content:
00:05 About 25,000 years ago, a group of people left central Europe carrying reindeer hides and stone tools. They were not fleeing predators. They were fleeing the cold. Even in summer, the ground no longer had enough time to thaw completely. Trees grew increasingly [music] sparse. The great herds had changed direction.
00:44 They did not know that the world around them was entering one of the harshest periods of the last ice age. They only knew that if they stayed, they would die. But ice did not [music] only drive life away. It once lowered the oceans, connected continents, and opened grasslands [music] that sustained giant creatures.
01:19 What ended the ice age? [groaning] And why were most of those giant species unable to survive when Earth warmed again. [music] As the ice age entered its coldest phase, Earth looked completely different. The global average temperature was about 6° C lower than it is today. That number may not seem very large, but it was enough to alter the climate, coastlines, and distribution of life [music] across the entire planet.
02:06 Much of northern Europe and Canada lay beneath enormous continental [music] ice sheets. In some places, the ice was up to 3 kilometers thick. They did not float on the ocean, but rested directly [music] on the land, pressing down on the continents with a weight whose traces are still recorded in the geology. But the greatest change did not occur only on land.
02:40 The water that formed those ice sheets was drawn from the oceans. Sea water evaporated, moved through the atmosphere, and then fell over the polar regions and mountains [music] as snow. Instead of melting and flowing back into the sea, this water remained trapped in ice for thousands of years. The more water was locked away on land, the lower the ocean level fell.
03:14 At the coldest point, sea level was about 120 m lower than it is today. Coastlines retreated. Shallow seafloors were exposed, connecting many land areas that are now separated by the ocean. The English Channel between England and France disappeared. In place [music] of the water was a plane crossed by rivers and valleys where herds [music] of mammoths could move from Europe into the land that is now the island of Great Britain.
03:53 In Southeast Asia, many islands were connected [music] to the mainland, forming a vast land mass known as Sunderland. In northeast Asia, Siberia and Alaska were also no longer separated [music] by the sea. Between the two regions appeared a land mass about 1,000 km wide called Bingia. Bingia was not a small narrow passage.
04:25 It was a cold, dry step that could still support life with rivers [music] and coldresistant grasses. For thousands of years, animals could [music] move between Asia and North America across this land. Later, humans followed the same route. However, the ice age was not a single [music] winter that continued without interruption.
04:55 The pleaene began about 2.6 million years ago and passed through many different cold and warm cycles. These cycles lasted tens of thousands of years and were influenced [music] by slow changes in Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis, and the direction in which its rotational [music] axis pointed through space.
05:17 When summers in the northern hemisphere became cooler, snow from the previous [music] winter did not melt completely. The snow continued to accumulate year after year. Its white surface [music] reflected more sunlight back into space, causing Earth to grow even colder. It also expanded the land, creating new migration corridors and cold grasslands that stretched across multiple continents.
05:50 That world was harsh, but it was far from empty. Across the newly opened grasslands, giant creatures began to dominate the landscape. Across the [music] cold grasslands stretching through Europe, Siberia, and Bingia, an extraordinarily diverse animal community took shape. giant creatures coexisted in a world that no place today can fully recreate.
06:28 The most prominent was the woolly mammoth, mammoth primogenius. It was not simply an elephant covered with extra fur. The mammoth's entire body was adapted to the prolonged cold of the northern step. The outer coat was long and coarse, reaching nearly 1 meter on some parts of the body. Beneath it was a shorter, dense layer of fur close to the skin.
07:02 Under the skin was also a layer of fat up to about 10 cm thick, providing both insulation and energy reserves. [music] On the Siberian step, winter temperatures could fall to minus40° C. Under those conditions, mammoths still had to find enough food to sustain their enormous bodies. Their upward curving tusks were not used only to display strength.
07:39 In mature males, they could grow longer than 4 m. Mammoths used their tusks to sweep aside snow and ice, reaching the dry grass that remained underneath. Their large mers crushed grasses and tough vegetation. An adult could eat between 180 and 220 kg of vegetation each day. In large numbers, mammoth herds placed considerable pressure on the landscape.
08:17 As they moved, they trampled vegetation, broke young trees, and opened clearings much as African elephants alter the savannah today. Mammoths did not live alone. Sharing the cold grasslands with them was the woolly rhinoceros sealodont antiquitatis. Its body was low, heavy, and covered with thick fur. On its head were two keratin horns with the front horn sometimes growing longer than 1.5 m.
09:00 The raised shoulder hump stored fat for the long winters. Unlike mammoths, which often traveled in groups, woolly rhinoceroses were largely solitary. Megallosceros also lived across these same lands and is commonly known as the Irish elk. Although its range extended from Ireland to China, the antlers of males could span about 3.5 m and weigh more than 40 kg.
09:33 For a long time, their size was considered the reason Megalosceros became extinct. One hypothesis suggested that as forests expanded at the end of the ice age, the oversized antlers made it difficult for males to move among the trees. However, the disappearance of this species was far more complex. Where herds of herbivores gathered, predators also appeared across the plains of Europe and Asia.
extract_chars_prompt:
You are an expert biological reference analyst and visual asset researcher.

Analyze the provided script and extract every distinct visual subject that appears or is meaningfully described.

A subject includes:
- Animals (extinct or extant species)
- Humans or human lineages
- Prehistoric creatures
- Plants or ecological subjects if they are important visual elements
- Large environmental entities only if they have a distinct physical form and may need visual reference
- Any other organism or physical entity that would require a consistent visual representation in a documentary, CGI scene, or AI-generated footage

Your task is NOT to summarize the script.
Your task is to build a reliable visual reference database for every subject.

For each subject, determine:

1. Identity
- Use the most scientifically accurate common name.
- Include scientific name when available.
- Distinguish closely related species or genera when the script mentions them.
- Do not merge different species into one generic category.

2. Physical appearance
Extract only stable biological characteristics:
- Overall body shape
- Body proportions
- Anatomy
- Distinctive features
- Fur, skin, feathers, scales, shells, horns, tusks, claws, teeth, limbs, tails, facial structure
- Sexual dimorphism if visually important
- Adaptations related to survival

Prioritize characteristics that affect visual generation accuracy.

3. Size and scale reference
Determine realistic adult size ranges based on scientific knowledge.

Include:
- The most relevant body measurement
- Typical adult size range
- Maximum size only when scientifically supported
- Mass range
- The best visual comparison measurement for cinematic scale matching

Avoid exaggerated descriptions.
Do not increase size because the creature is famous or dramatic.

4. Visual identity constraints
Provide information that prevents incorrect generation:
- What the subject should NOT look like
- Common misconceptions
- Similar species it could be confused with
- Important scale limitations

Examples:
- "Large prehistoric cat, but not tiger-sized"
- "Giant spider visually large but still much smaller than mammals"
- "Human ancestor with powerful build, not modern human proportions"

5. Documentary realism requirements
The reference must represent realistic scientific interpretation.

Avoid:
- Fantasy traits
- Movie monster characteristics
- Exaggerated muscles
- Incorrect colors
- Unrealistic anatomy
- Modern animal features applied to extinct species without evidence

6. Visual generation usefulness
Focus on details useful for:
- AI image generation
- CGI modeling
- 3D asset creation
- Documentary footage matching
- Shot composition and scale comparison

7. Completeness requirement
Do not skip subjects because they appear briefly.

Extract all important entities mentioned throughout the script, including:
- Main subjects
- Secondary subjects
- Predators
- Prey animals
- Human groups
- Organisms involved in ecological interactions

If a subject appears multiple times, consolidate all information into one complete reference profile.

Ignore:
- Locations
- Historical events
- Abstract concepts
- Climate processes
- Geological events

unless they represent a physical visual subject.

Maintain scientific uncertainty:
- If exact values are unknown, provide reasonable scientific ranges.
- If a characteristic is debated, indicate uncertainty instead of inventing details.

The final result should function as a professional reference library for creating consistent documentary visuals from this script.

characters.name: Homo sapiens — Pleistocene hunter-gatherer
characters.description: Anatomically modern human with an upright bipedal body, relatively long limbs, a comparatively narrow trunk, high rounded cranial vault, near-vertical forehead, reduced brow ridges, and a lightly projecting face. Skin, hair, and eye pigmentation varied among populations; there is no single universal Ice Age appearance. Upper Paleolithic people should look biologically modern, not apelike or cartoonishly primitive.

size_profile.scale_notes: Adult humans are small beside mammoths, rhinoceroses, and bison. Clothing, hides, and tools alter the silhouette but not the underlying biological proportions. Clovis-associated people are Homo sapiens, not a separate human species.

characters.motion_profile: Efficient upright biped capable of walking, running, climbing, throwing, fine hand manipulation, endurance travel, and coordinated spear use.
characters.behavior_profile: Lives in mobile cooperative groups; hunts, processes food, works hides, uses fire and lamps, creates symbolic markings, and follows seasonal animal migrations. Social organization and technology are important visual cues, but the people should not be depicted as uniformly muscular or culturally identical.

characters.name: Neanderthal — Homo neanderthalensis
characters.description: Short, broad, robust human lineage with a deep thorax, broad pelvis, thick limb bones, relatively short distal limbs, heavy musculature, a long low cranial vault, strong brow ridges, large midface, broad nose, projecting jaws, and a weak chin. The face is distinctive but still recognizably human. Do not depict Neanderthals as hunched apemen, primitive caricatures, or uniformly covered in body hair.

size_profile.scale_notes: Typical reconstructed adults are shorter and heavier-built than many modern humans, but height overlaps modern human variation. Use a powerful compact build rather than exaggerated bodybuilder muscles.

characters.motion_profile: Powerful upright biped capable of walking, running, climbing, throwing, close-range grappling, and repeated heavy-load movement. Limb proportions favor compact power rather than long-distance sprinting.
characters.behavior_profile: Cooperative hunter of large mammals; made sophisticated stone tools, used fire and shelters, wore clothing, and may have practiced burial and symbolic behavior. Group hunting should look coordinated and physically demanding, not technologically helpless.

characters.name: Denisovan — archaic Homo lineage
characters.description: Denisovans are known from fragmentary fossils and ancient DNA, so no secure complete adult reconstruction exists. The most defensible visual model is a Pleistocene Homo with an upright human body and potentially variable robustness. Facial structure, body proportions, and pigmentation remain uncertain. Do not give Denisovans a standardized fantasy phenotype or assume that one inferred pigmentation profile represents the entire lineage.

size_profile.scale_notes: The numerical range is a working proxy based on Pleistocene Homo, not a secure species-specific measurement. Keep Denisovans within plausible human scale and avoid making them dramatically larger or more primitive than Neanderthals or Homo sapiens.

characters.motion_profile: Likely upright bipedal human locomotion, including walking, running, climbing, tool use, and carrying; exact locomotor specialization is unknown.
characters.behavior_profile: Associated with an Asian and Siberian human lineage that interbred with Neanderthals and Homo sapiens. Specific toolmaking and cultural assignments are often uncertain because fossils and archaeological contexts are limited.

characters.name: Reindeer or caribou — Rangifer tarandus
characters.description: Medium-sized deer with a compact barrel-shaped body, relatively long legs, short tail, large concave hooves, thick multilayered fur with hollow insulating hairs, and pale areas around the neck, rump, and lower limbs. Both sexes grow antlers; males usually have much larger and more elaborate antlers. Do not depict them as red deer or elk, and do not use domesticated reindeer traits as the only model for wild Pleistocene animals.

size_profile.scale_notes: Large bulls can exceed 200 kg, but reindeer are still much smaller than bison, rhinoceroses, or mammoths. Antler size is strongly sex- and season-dependent.

characters.motion_profile: Efficient quadrupedal walker and runner capable of long-distance migration, bounding over uneven ground, moving through snow, and swimming.
characters.behavior_profile: Highly gregarious grazer and mixed feeder that forms seasonal herds and follows predictable migration routes. Reindeer are plausible prey for cave lions and important food for Paleolithic people.

characters.name: Woolly mammoth — Mammuthus primigenius
characters.description: Large elephantid with a high shoulder, strongly sloping back, domed head, small ears, short tail, trunk, and long spiral-curving tusks. The coat consisted of long coarse guard hair over a dense shorter underfur, with substantial subcutaneous fat. Hair was probably dark brown to chocolate-brown rather than uniformly orange or white. Molars were high-crowned and ridged for grinding abrasive grasses. Do not make it a modern African elephant with enormous ears, a flat back, or straight tusks.

size_profile.scale_notes: Typical adults were about 3–3.5 m at the shoulder and roughly 4–6 tonnes. Mature male tusks could exceed 4 m, but tusk length varied widely and should not be used to imply an oversized body. Woolly mammoths were large elephants, not dinosaur-scale animals.

characters.motion_profile: Elephant-like walking with a slow powerful gait; uses trunk for feeding and tusks for sweeping snow, manipulating vegetation, and digging through frozen ground.
characters.behavior_profile: Herbivorous grazer living in family herds, with adult males potentially more solitary. Herd movement trampled vegetation, broke shrubs and young trees, and helped maintain open grasslands. Daily food intake was measured in hundreds of kilograms of vegetation.

characters.name: Woolly rhinoceros — Coelodonta antiquitatis
characters.description: Low-slung, deep-bodied rhinoceros with short stocky legs, a thick two-layer coat of coarse guard hair and dense underfur, small ears, a broad head, and a raised shoulder hump containing fat and muscle. The front horn was broad, laterally compressed, and sometimes approached 1.5 m; a smaller rear horn was present. Do not depict a hairless modern rhinoceros or a single-horned unicorn-like animal.

size_profile.scale_notes: Comparable in overall mass to a large modern rhinoceros, not dramatically larger. The horn is keratin, not bone, and should have a flattened scraping profile rather than a smooth conical spike.

characters.motion_profile: Heavy quadrupedal walking and trotting; capable of forceful head movements and horn-driven snow scraping.
characters.behavior_profile: Primarily a solitary cold-steppe grazer. It could sweep snow aside with the broad front horn to reach grasses and other low vegetation.

characters.name: Giant deer or Irish elk — Megaloceros giganteus
characters.description: Very large deer with long limbs, a deep torso, elongated neck, and strongly built male shoulders and neck. Mature males carried enormous palmated antlers; females lacked antlers. A shoulder hump and powerful neck musculature are plausible, but the animal should remain deer-like rather than moose-like. Coat color is uncertain and should remain within natural brown, gray-brown, or seasonal deer ranges.

size_profile.scale_notes: The body was approximately elk-sized; the spectacular scale came mainly from the male antlers, which could span about 3.5 m and weigh more than 40 kg. Do not give females male antlers or make the body as large as a moose.

characters.motion_profile: Long-striding quadrupedal runner capable of sustained movement across open parkland and grassland.
characters.behavior_profile: Herbivorous deer using open grassland and parkland rather than dense forest. Males likely displayed, paraded, and fought with antlers during the breeding season.

characters.name: Cave lion — Panthera spelaea
characters.description: Large pantherine cat with a long muscular torso, powerful limbs, broad skull, large paws, and a long tail. The coat was probably tawny or pale brown, possibly with subtle patterning. Paleolithic art commonly shows males without a large mane, but mane development remains uncertain. Do not default to a modern African lion with a heavy mane, and do not give it saber teeth.

size_profile.scale_notes: Late Pleistocene cave lions were generally large but not uniformly gigantic. Earlier cave-lion forms were larger, while some late populations were smaller. Use a size modestly above many modern lions, not a 400–500 kg default.

characters.motion_profile: Stalking quadruped capable of short explosive acceleration, pouncing, grappling, and powerful bites; not specialized for prolonged high-speed pursuit.
characters.behavior_profile: Predator of reindeer, steppe bison, and other large herbivores. Group hunting and social structure are uncertain; do not automatically depict an African-style pride.

characters.name: Steppe bison — Bison priscus
characters.description: Large wild bovid with massive forequarters, a pronounced shoulder hump, broad head, thick neck, long outward-curving horns, and a dense shaggy coat. The coat was probably dark brown to nearly black with regional and seasonal variation. The body often had a smooth double-humped outline caused by the shoulder and pelvis. Do not depict domestic cattle or a modern plains bison with no regional variation.

size_profile.scale_notes: Steppe bison were often somewhat larger and more long-horned than living bison, but size varied across the Pleistocene. They remain bison-sized, not rhinoceros-sized.

characters.motion_profile: Heavy quadrupedal walking and powerful galloping; capable of abrupt herd turns, horn clashes, and forceful charges.
characters.behavior_profile: Gregarious grazer living in herds and occupying open steppe and forest-steppe. It was important prey for cave lions and a major target of human hunting.

characters.name: Cave bear — Ursus spelaeus
characters.description: Massive bear with a long body, high shoulder hump, large head, powerful forelimbs, short tail, and dense brown or brown-black fur. The skull and molars were strongly adapted for processing plant material. Do not make it a polar bear, a short-faced bear, or an obligate meat-eating cave monster.

size_profile.scale_notes: Large males could exceed 500 kg. The animal should be massive but still bear-proportioned, with a lower and more robust profile than a modern polar bear.

characters.motion_profile: Plantigrade quadrupedal walking, digging, climbing when necessary, and standing or rearing briefly. Hibernation involves prolonged inactivity in sheltered cavities.
characters.behavior_profile: Predominantly herbivorous, feeding on grasses, roots, leaves, and fruits; regional omnivory remains debated. Repeated cave use for hibernation brought cave bears into occasional conflict with humans.

characters.name: North American saber-toothed cat — Smilodon fatalis
characters.description: Low-slung, short-tailed, extremely robust cat with massive forequarters, thick neck, broad skull, powerful forelimbs, relatively short hind limbs, and very long laterally flattened upper canines. Canines could approach 28 cm. Fur color and pattern are unknown, so use restrained tawny, brown, gray, or muted spotted possibilities rather than fixed tiger striping. Do not make it a long-legged lion or tiger.

size_profile.scale_notes: Typical estimates overlap the mass of a large tiger. The animal is visually heavy and front-loaded, but not a giant bear-sized cat by default. Do not place the canines outside the closed mouth in a permanently exposed fantasy pose.

characters.motion_profile: Ambush predator capable of short explosive bursts, pouncing, pinning prey with the forelimbs, and delivering a precise neck bite; poorly suited to prolonged pursuit.
characters.behavior_profile: Probably specialized in attacking large prey at close range. Sociality, cooperative hunting, and the extent of group living remain uncertain and should not be treated as settled facts.

characters.name: South American saber-toothed cat — Smilodon populator
characters.description: The largest Smilodon species, with an exceptionally deep and broad chest, massive forelimbs, heavy neck muscles, short tail, broad skull, and long saber canines. It was more powerfully built than Smilodon fatalis and should not be merged with the North American species. Fur pattern and color remain uncertain.

size_profile.scale_notes: Typical estimates fall around 220–360 kg, while exceptionally large individuals may have exceeded 400 kg. Do not make every individual 400 kg or depict it as a normal lion with oversized teeth.

characters.motion_profile: Short-range ambush predator relying on concealment, explosive movement, forelimb restraint, and a controlled saber-tooth bite rather than sustained running.
characters.behavior_profile: Likely attacked large South American herbivores. Sociality and cooperative hunting are unresolved; use cautious, species-typical feline behavior rather than assuming a lion-like pride.

characters.name: Giant ground sloth — Megatherium americanum
characters.description: Huge ground-dwelling sloth with a barrel-shaped torso, massive pelvis, columnar limbs, broad plantigrade feet, a relatively small head, and very long curved foreclaws. Its body was heavily built for terrestrial support, not tree climbing. Soft-tissue color, fur density, and facial details are uncertain; use coarse hair or sparse shaggy covering rather than a modern tree-sloth coat.

size_profile.scale_notes: The approximately 6 m figure refers to total body extent or an elevated posture, not ordinary shoulder height. It was enormous, but should remain a ground sloth rather than an elephant with claws.

characters.motion_profile: Slow but powerful quadrupedal movement; could rear onto the hind limbs and tail, using the forelimbs and claws to pull down branches.
characters.behavior_profile: Large herbivorous browser capable of feeding on elevated foliage from a reared posture. It was not an arboreal sloth and should not move like a modern tree-dweller.

characters.name: Glyptodon — Glyptodon spp.
characters.description: Large quadrupedal glyptodont with a domed rigid carapace made from fused bony osteoderms, a small head, stout limbs, and a heavily armored tail ending in a bony tube or club-like structure. The shell should appear as a continuous biological armor surface rather than a turtle shell. Do not use the extremely massive tail club of Doedicurus as the default Glyptodon condition.

size_profile.scale_notes: Large specimens could approach two tonnes, but the genus included size variation. It was much larger than a modern armadillo while remaining low and broad rather than tall.

characters.motion_profile: Slow, low quadrupedal walking with limited agility; could swing the armored tail defensively.
characters.behavior_profile: Herbivorous grazer or mixed feeder. The carapace provided passive defense, while tail use in combat or predator defense is plausible but not fully resolved for every species.

characters.name: Terror birds — Phorusrhacidae
characters.description: Family-level group of mostly flightless predatory birds with large laterally compressed hooked beaks, long powerful legs, reduced wings, and feathered bodies. The family was highly variable, ranging from relatively small forms to very large species over 2 m tall. Do not depict them as featherless dinosaurs, toothed birds, or one uniform giant species.

size_profile.scale_notes: These are family-level estimates, not a single species profile. The largest terror birds were much bigger than modern seriemas, but many phorusrhacids were substantially smaller. Most giant lineages had already declined before the late Pleistocene.

characters.motion_profile: Cursorial terrestrial running with rapid head and neck strikes; wing reduction favors balance and maneuvering rather than sustained flight.
characters.behavior_profile: Predatory birds occupying terrestrial carnivore niches. Diet, speed, sociality, and hunting technique varied by species and should not be generalized from one famous giant form.

characters.name: American mastodon — Mammut americanum
characters.description: Large proboscidean with a long low-held head, broad body, columnar limbs, gently curved tusks, and a shaggy insulating coat. Its molars had rounded cone-like cusps suited to browsing twigs, shrubs, and other woody vegetation rather than the ridged grazing teeth of mammoths. Do not confuse it with a woolly mammoth: the head is lower, the tusks are less spiral, and the body is generally more woodland-adapted.

size_profile.scale_notes: Many adults were approximately elephant-sized, with some large males reaching several tonnes beyond 5,000 kg. Do not make every mastodon as tall or heavily furred as a woolly mammoth.

characters.motion_profile: Elephant-like quadrupedal walking through woodland and wet ground; uses trunk and tusks for browsing and manipulation.
characters.behavior_profile: Primarily a browser of shrubs, trees, and wetland vegetation. Females may have lived socially while adult males could be more solitary, as in living elephant relatives.

characters.name: American camel — Camelops hesternus
characters.description: Large North American camelid with a long neck, long limbs, two-toed feet, deep body, and camel-like head. A hump is not securely known and should not be added as a certainty. Fur color, density, and facial soft tissue are also uncertain. Do not depict it as a modern dromedary with a guaranteed single hump or as a small llama.

size_profile.scale_notes: A representative adult was roughly 2.1–2.2 m at the shoulder and around 800 kg, with regional variation. Keep it large and long-legged but below mammoth or mastodon mass.

characters.motion_profile: Long-striding quadrupedal walking and running; capable of efficient movement across open ground and varied terrain.
characters.behavior_profile: Probably traveled in groups and fed on a mixture of grasses, shrubs, and other plants. Exact social behavior and hump morphology remain uncertain.

characters.name: Pleistocene North American horse — Equus spp., with Equus scotti as a representative
characters.description: One-toed wild equid with compact horse-like proportions, sturdy limbs, an elongated head, upright mane, and long tail. Coat colors are unknown and should remain within natural dun, brown, black, or muted patterned ranges. Do not use domestic breeds, saddles, bridles, or exaggerated draft-horse musculature.

size_profile.scale_notes: The script does not identify one exact species; Equus scotti is a useful large representative. North American Pleistocene Equus taxonomy is complex, and several species or morphotypes may have been present.

characters.motion_profile: Efficient quadrupedal walking, trotting, and galloping with a one-toed hoof; capable of rapid herd movement over open terrain.
characters.behavior_profile: Grazing herbivore that likely lived in small or moderate-sized herds. It should behave like a wary wild equid, not a domesticated riding horse.

characters.name: Pleistocene Eurasian wild horse — Equus spp.
characters.description: Sturdy one-toed wild equid with a compact barrel, long lower limbs, upright mane, and long tail. The exact species is not specified in the script, so use a generalized Pleistocene Eurasian horse rather than a modern domestic breed. Coat colors may include dun, bay, brown, black, or muted striping, but no single pattern is certain.

size_profile.scale_notes: Use a medium-sized wild horse, generally smaller than mammoths and bison. Exact Pleistocene horse taxonomy and body size varied by region; avoid modern Thoroughbred or pony proportions.

characters.motion_profile: Quadrupedal walking, trotting, and fast galloping; capable of sustained herd travel and sudden flight from predators.
characters.behavior_profile: Gregarious grazing herbivore following seasonal forage. Wild, alert behavior is more appropriate than domesticated responsiveness.

characters.name: Mammoth-steppe or steppe-tundra ecosystem
characters.description: Cold, dry open grassland mosaic containing grasses, sedges, flowering forbs, dwarf shrubs, patches of bare soil, shallow snow, and occasional sparse trees or shrub thickets. It should look productive and biologically rich, not like a featureless white desert. The ecosystem supported dense herds of large grazers.

size_profile.scale_notes: Landscape-scale biome extending across portions of Eurasia and North America. It was a variable mosaic rather than a uniform habitat with identical vegetation everywhere.

characters.motion_profile: Vegetation moves with wind and seasonal growth; snow cover accumulates and thins; rivers and shallow channels may cross the open ground.
characters.behavior_profile: Maintained partly by grazing, trampling, browsing, and nutrient return from megaherbivores. Loss of the large herds allowed shrubs, tundra, and forest to expand in many regions.

characters.name: Cold-resistant steppe grasses, sedges, and forbs
characters.description: Low herbaceous ground cover dominated by tufted grasses, sedges, drought- and frost-tolerant herbs, and flowering forbs. Vegetation should appear patchy, dense near moist ground, and generally green-brown-gold depending on season. Include occasional dwarf shrubs, but do not turn the steppe into a modern lawn.

size_profile.scale_notes: Individual plants are low; cinematic scale comes from broad continuous ground cover and the presence of large herbivore herds. The exact species composition varied across Eurasia and Beringia.

characters.motion_profile: Plants grow seasonally, bend in wind, shed seeds, and regrow from perennial roots or rhizomes.
characters.behavior_profile: Primary forage for mammoths, horses, bison, reindeer, and other herbivores. Dense grazing and trampling can preserve an open grassland structure.

characters.name: Arctic and subarctic tundra vegetation
characters.description: Low treeless plant community of mosses, lichens, sedges, dwarf shrubs, and small forbs growing over shallow active soil and frozen ground. It should look textured and biologically alive, not like bare ice. Dense tree cover is inappropriate for the core tundra visual.

size_profile.scale_notes: Vegetation height is low, but tundra can extend across very large continuous landscapes. Distinguish shrub tundra from the taller, more productive mammoth-steppe grassland.

characters.motion_profile: Slow seasonal growth, wind movement, flowering, seed release, and winter dormancy.
characters.behavior_profile: Provides forage and cover for reindeer and smaller organisms. Expansion of tundra into former grassland reduced the continuous grazing habitat available to megafauna.

characters.name: Pleistocene northern boreal forest and expanding woodland
characters.description: Patchy woodland of conifers, birch, willow, and other cold-tolerant trees with shrubs, leaf litter, open glades, and shaded ground. During forest expansion it should often appear as a mosaic or parkland rather than an impenetrable modern forest. Do not use tropical rainforest structure for northern Europe or Siberia.

size_profile.scale_notes: Individual trees may range from small shrubs to roughly 25 m, while the ecological entity is landscape-scale. Forest expansion fragmented the open steppe corridors used by large grazers.

characters.motion_profile: Trees grow slowly, sway in wind, shed leaves or needles, and spread through seedling establishment and vegetative growth.
characters.behavior_profile: Provides browse, shelter, and shade but reduces continuous open grazing habitat. Increasing woodland is a major visual contrast with the earlier mammoth-steppe landscape.

characters.name: Continental ice sheet
characters.description: Grounded continent-scale ice mass with layered blue-white ice, snow accumulation zones, crevasses, flow lines, pressure ridges, and outlet glaciers. It rests directly on land and should not be represented as floating sea ice. Ice sheets should dominate the horizon through scale rather than through sharp fantasy mountains of ice.

size_profile.scale_notes: Last-glacial ice sheets covered continental regions and reached thicknesses approaching 3 km in some areas. Their visual scale is thousands of kilometres, with local thickness measured in kilometres.

characters.motion_profile: Flows extremely slowly as a massive grounded body, feeding outlet glaciers and ice streams; crevasses and ice fronts change over long timescales.
characters.behavior_profile: Stores enormous quantities of frozen freshwater and presses down on the underlying land. Its extent controls migration corridors, coastlines, and the location of ice-free passages.

characters.name: Beringia or the Bering land bridge
characters.description: Broad exposed landmass connecting northeastern Asia and Alaska during low sea level. It should appear as a cold, dry, mostly ice-free steppe-tundra landscape with rivers, lowlands, shrubs, forbs, permafrost, and occasional lakes. It was not a narrow rocky footbridge or a submerged-looking island chain.

size_profile.scale_notes: The exposed region was a landscape-scale subcontinent, more than 1,000 km across in some reconstructions and far larger than a simple corridor. Use broad horizons and continuous terrain.

characters.motion_profile: Static land surface shaped by rivers, wind, seasonal snow, permafrost thaw, and long-term shoreline change.
characters.behavior_profile: Served as habitat and migration terrain for mammoths, horses, bison, reindeer, humans, and other organisms before rising sea levels submerged it.

characters.name: Sundaland or the exposed Sunda Shelf
characters.description: Low-relief exposed continental shelf joining mainland Southeast Asia with Sumatra, Java, Borneo, and adjacent land during glacial low sea levels. The landscape could include broad river systems, wetlands, savanna, woodland, and forest mosaics. It should not be shown as the modern island chain separated by deep ocean channels.

size_profile.scale_notes: The exposed shelf formed a very large landmass, with an area of several million square kilometres. Exact coastline and vegetation changed through the glacial cycle.

characters.motion_profile: Static continental shelf crossed by rivers, wetlands, seasonal floodplains, and changing coastlines as sea level rises or falls.
characters.behavior_profile: Created terrestrial migration routes between parts of Southeast Asia that are now separated by shallow seas. It is a physical paleolandscape, not a lost city or artificial continent.

characters.name: Pleistocene North Sea–English Channel plain or Doggerland
characters.description: Low-lying exposed shelf connecting Britain with continental Europe, containing rivers, valleys, wetlands, grasslands, and shallow lakes. It should look like a terrestrial plain crossed by herds, not like an ocean channel. Its exact local topography varied through time.

size_profile.scale_notes: Regional scale ranged from tens to hundreds of kilometres. Use low relief, braided watercourses, and open herbivore habitat rather than dramatic mountains.

characters.motion_profile: Rivers migrate, wetlands flood and drain, and coastlines shift as sea level changes.
characters.behavior_profile: Provided terrestrial movement routes for mammoths, humans, and other animals before marine flooding separated Britain from continental Europe.

characters.name: Pleistocene permafrost ground
characters.description: Frozen mineral soil and sediment containing ice lenses and organic matter beneath a shallow seasonally thawed surface. The visible ground may be dry, cracked, gravelly, grass-covered, or snow-patched. It should not be confused with a solid glacier or permanent deep snowfield.

size_profile.scale_notes: Permafrost is a subsurface condition extending across broad regions; the active thaw layer is much shallower than the frozen ground beneath it. Local thickness varies substantially.

characters.motion_profile: Mostly static on human timescales, with seasonal thaw, cracking, subsidence, and slow release of trapped water and organic material.
characters.behavior_profile: Supports tundra and steppe vegetation and preserves bones, tusks, hair, and other organic remains. Thawing can destabilize the surface and alter drainage.

characters.name: Proglacial lake and ice dam
characters.description: Large freshwater lake ponded against a glacier or ice-sheet margin, held back by a steep wall or ridge of compacted ice. Water should appear cold, sediment-laden, and potentially braided toward an outlet. Do not depict the dam as a permanent rock wall or the lake as a normal modern alpine lake.

size_profile.scale_notes: Individual lakes and ice dams varied greatly; use kilometre-scale water bodies and ice walls rather than small ponds when illustrating the script's sudden freshwater discharge.

characters.motion_profile: Water accumulates, circulates, drains through channels, and can breach or overtop the ice dam rapidly compared with the slow movement of the surrounding ice sheet.
characters.behavior_profile: A physical glacial feature that can release large pulses of freshwater when the ice barrier fails. It is not a biological subject and should be rendered as an unstable temporary landscape element.

characters.name: Paleolithic cave and rock shelter
characters.description: Natural cave entrance, limestone overhang, or shallow rock shelter with irregular stone surfaces, dark interior spaces, soot staining, sediment floors, and sheltered ledges. It should look geologically natural and uneven, not like a constructed house or a uniformly smooth fantasy cavern.

size_profile.scale_notes: Entrances and chambers range from human-scale niches to large halls. The visual reference should preserve a clear human scale through crouching, standing, lamps, and animal remains.

characters.motion_profile: Static physical structure; smoke, firelight, dripping water, and wind may animate the interior.
characters.behavior_profile: Used by humans as refuge, working space, ritual or symbolic-marking location, and sometimes contested shelter shared with cave bears.

characters.name: Paleolithic flint-and-bone tool assemblage
characters.description: Collection of chipped flint spear points, long stone blades, scrapers, engraving tools, bone needles with pierced eyes, and spear throwers. Stone edges should be irregularly knapped and functional, while bone tools should show polished working surfaces and organic curvature. Do not use metal blades, modern machined symmetry, or fantasy weapons.

size_profile.scale_notes: Most individual tools are hand-sized; spear shafts and spear throwers create longer silhouettes. The assemblage is small relative to the people and animals using it.

characters.motion_profile: Stationary when stored; manipulated through cutting, scraping, piercing, engraving, throwing, and hafting.
characters.behavior_profile: Represents technological planning, hide processing, hunting at distance, sewing, and bone or antler working. Tool form should vary by task rather than appearing as one standardized kit.

characters.name: Paleolithic hide clothing and hide shelters
characters.description: Fitted garments, wraps, blankets, and temporary tents made from sewn animal hides or skins, with visible seams, lacing, folds, fur direction, and layered insulation. Clothing should fit closely enough for movement and thermal protection. Do not use woven modern fabric, metal fasteners, fantasy fur armor, or a single universal costume.

size_profile.scale_notes: Garments follow human body scale; hide tents or blankets can span several metres. Hide type, fur retention, cut, and decoration varied by region and period.

characters.motion_profile: Flexible material that folds, stretches, flaps in wind, and moves with the wearer; tent hides can billow or sag over frames.
characters.behavior_profile: Provides insulation, weather protection, bedding, and portable shelter. Hide preparation involves scraping, stretching, sewing, and repeated repair.

characters.name: Mammoth-bone shelter framework
characters.description: Temporary shelter frame made from large mammoth ribs, limb bones, vertebrae, and sometimes tusks or ivory, with hides stretched over the structure. Bones should retain irregular natural shapes, porous ends, and large elephantid proportions. Do not depict it as a permanent wooden house or a structure made from small generic animal bones.

size_profile.scale_notes: The shelter is human-occupiable and several metres across; individual mammoth ribs and limb bones may be over 1 m long. The structure remains low and temporary.

characters.motion_profile: Static frame; attached hides can flex, flap, and sag with wind or use.
characters.behavior_profile: Constructed from scavenged or butchered mammoth remains to provide shelter, working space, and possibly fuel material. It is a human-made assembly, not a natural mammoth skeleton pile.

characters.name: Paleolithic cave art and mineral pigments
characters.description: Wall-bound images and marks made with red ochre, black manganese minerals, charcoal, and related pigments. Common animal forms include mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, cave lions, bison, horses, and deer, often shown in profile with carefully observed anatomy and movement. Do not render the art as modern oil painting, cartoon illustration, or perfectly flat digital graphics.

size_profile.scale_notes: Individual figures may be tens of centimetres to over a metre across, while decorated chambers can extend many metres. Pigment is uneven, weathered, and integrated with natural rock relief.

characters.motion_profile: Static imagery; candle or fat-lamp light creates moving shadows across the uneven wall surface.
characters.behavior_profile: Records symbolic representation, observation of animal anatomy, and repeated use of cave walls for marking. The images should preserve archaeological irregularity rather than appearing newly painted.

characters.name: Paleolithic human footprints in wet sediment
characters.description: Preserved impressions of human feet with heel, arch, forefoot, and toe pressure arranged in a trackway. The prints should be anatomically human and embedded in layered wet sediment that later hardened or was buried. They are not fossilized bones, carved symbols, or tool marks.

size_profile.scale_notes: Individual adult footprints are roughly human foot length; the important visual scale comes from spacing, stride direction, and the surrounding sediment surface.

characters.motion_profile: No living motion remains; the trackway records sequential bipedal walking across wet ground.
characters.behavior_profile: Physical evidence of human movement through an Ice Age landscape. The trackway should preserve natural variation in depth, toe pressure, stride length, and partial erosion.

extract_shots_prompt:
You are an expert wildlife documentary cinematographer, visual coverage planner, and physical scene analyst.

Analyze the provided documentary script and convert it into a HIGH-DENSITY sequence of physically achievable single continuous video shots suitable for immediate AI video generation.

Your goal is NOT to rewrite or summarize the script.

Your goal is to extract ALL useful visual beats required to visually cover the narration with enough shot variation for professional documentary editing.

==================================================
PRIMARY SHOT-DENSITY RULE
=========================

Generate approximately ONE shot for every 5–8 seconds of finished video.

Assume each generated video clip will normally last about 8 seconds.

For a 10-minute script, target approximately 70–80 shots.

DO NOT compress an entire sentence, paragraph, concept, animal behavior sequence, or environmental transition into one shot if it can reasonably be represented by multiple distinct visual beats.

A single narration sentence may require:

* 1 shot
* 2 shots
* 3 shots
* 4 shots
* or more

depending on how many distinct visible events, details, spatial relationships, environmental changes, or scientific concepts it contains.

Err on the side of producing MORE usable shots rather than fewer.

Do not summarize visual coverage.

==================================================
VISUAL BEAT SEGMENTATION
========================

Before defining shots, mentally divide the narration into visual beats.

Create a new shot whenever there is a meaningful change in:

* subject
* action
* action phase
* subject scale
* subject-environment relationship
* spatial relationship
* geographic location
* environmental condition
* scientific detail
* anatomical detail
* behavior
* camera distance
* useful documentary emphasis

Do NOT require a narration sentence boundary to create a new shot.

One sentence may contain several shots.

Example:

Narration:
"Mammoths used their tusks to sweep aside snow and ice, reaching dry grass underneath."

Possible visual coverage:

Shot 1:
Wide establishing view of mammoth moving across snow-covered steppe.

Shot 2:
Medium side view as mammoth stops and lowers its head.

Shot 3:
Close view of tusks contacting the snow surface.

Shot 4:
Low close-up as a tusk pushes snow aside.

Shot 5:
Close-up of exposed dry grass beneath the removed snow.

Shot 6:
Medium view as the mammoth gathers the exposed vegetation.

These are separate physically continuous shots.

==================================================
DOCUMENTARY COVERAGE RULE
=========================

Whenever a subject, behavior, environment, or scientific concept is important, generate multiple complementary shots when physically justified.

Use documentary coverage such as:

* establishing shot
* wide behavioral shot
* medium behavioral shot
* close observational shot
* detail insert
* environmental insert
* reaction shot
* aftermath shot
* movement shot
* scale shot

Do not generate these mechanically.

Use them only when they provide genuinely different visual information.

==================================================
SHOT-SCALE VARIATION
====================

Avoid long sequences of identical framing.

Across adjacent shots, vary shot scale naturally:

Extreme Wide → Wide → Medium → Close-up → Medium → Wide

or another physically appropriate progression.

Use:

* extreme wide shots for geography, migration, ice sheets, exposed land, coastlines, herds
* wide shots for animal-environment relationships and movement
* medium shots for behavior
* close-ups for physical interaction, anatomy, tools, tracks, food, snow, tusks, vegetation, feet, hands
* macro shots only for genuinely small physical details

Do NOT artificially change framing if it makes the scientific content less clear.

==================================================
ENVIRONMENTAL COVERAGE
======================

Do not show only animals and humans.

Extract standalone environmental shots when the narration describes physical environmental processes.

Examples:

* frozen ground
* sparse tree line
* wind moving dry steppe grass
* snow accumulation
* glacial ice surface
* exposed river valleys
* retreating coastline
* shallow seafloor exposed as land
* meltwater channels
* snow covering vegetation
* ice pressing against rock
* broad migration corridors

Environmental processes should receive their own shots rather than being hidden inside animal shots.

==================================================
SCIENTIFIC PROCESS VISUALIZATION
================================

For narration describing large-scale natural processes, break the process into several physically plausible shots.

Example:
Water becomes trapped in continental ice.

Possible sequence:

1. Wide ocean surface under cold conditions.
2. Moist air and cloud formation over the ocean.
3. Snow falling over mountainous or polar terrain.
4. Snow accumulating over older snow.
5. Compressed snow becoming dense glacial ice.
6. Extreme wide view of expanding ice sheet.

Do not combine an entire multi-stage physical process into one impossible shot.

Do not use magical transitions or time-lapse unless explicitly requested.

Each shot must represent one observable phase.

==================================================
ANIMAL BEHAVIOR COVERAGE
========================

For important animal behavior, separate distinct physical phases.

For example:

Animal feeding may become:

* animal approaching feeding area
* animal lowering head
* physical contact with snow or vegetation
* vegetation becoming exposed
* animal collecting food
* animal chewing

Animal migration may become:

* distant herd movement
* medium group movement
* individual feet crossing terrain
* animals navigating an obstacle
* herd moving away into distance

Do not collapse an entire behavior sequence into one shot.

==================================================
HUMAN ACTIVITY COVERAGE
=======================

For prehistoric human scenes, divide visible activities into distinct shots when justified.

Examples:

* group walking across frozen terrain
* feet moving over hard ground
* person carrying folded hide
* stone tools hanging from or held by a traveler
* human examining frozen ground
* group crossing open grassland
* person looking toward distant herd
* group continuing migration

Do not show modern objects.

Do not invent unnecessary activities not supported by the narration.

==================================================
SHOT INDEPENDENCE
=================

Every generated shot must be independently usable as an 5–8 second AI-generated video clip.

Each shot must have:

* one coherent camera setup
* one readable primary visual idea
* physically continuous action
* no hidden edit
* no montage
* no multiple camera positions
* no teleportation
* no time jump inside the shot

The END of one shot may lead naturally into the NEXT shot.

==================================================
DO NOT MERGE VISUAL BEATS
=========================

Do not merge separate visual beats merely because they appear in the same sentence or paragraph.

For example, this narration:

"Trees became sparse. The ground remained frozen. Herds changed direction."

requires at least three distinct visual ideas:

* increasingly sparse trees
* frozen ground
* migrating herd changing direction

and may reasonably require several shots for each depending on importance.

==================================================
SHOT COUNT VALIDATION
=====================

After extracting the sequence, internally verify shot density.

Target:
approximately 7–8 shots per minute of narration.

Acceptable range:
approximately 6–10 shots per minute.

If a section of one minute contains only 1–3 shots, inspect it again and identify missing:

* environmental shots
* behavioral phases
* detail inserts
* establishing views
* transition shots
* scientific process stages
* changes in spatial relationship

Increase coverage until the visual sequence is sufficiently dense.

Do not inflate shot count with duplicate shots that communicate the same information.

==================================================
FOR EVERY SHOT, IDENTIFY
========================

1. Visible subjects

Extract only subjects physically visible inside the frame.

Include:

* animals
* humans
* physically present objects
* terrain features with direct physical presence

Do not include:

* mentioned but invisible subjects
* narration concepts
* historical references without physical representation
* abstract scientific concepts

A subject should appear only if a viewer could point to it on screen.

---

2. Cinematography analysis

Design ONE coherent camera setup that could realistically film the entire shot.

Describe:

Shot size:

* extreme wide shot
* wide shot
* medium shot
* close-up
* macro when appropriate

Camera position:

* ground level
* low angle
* elevated position
* aerial/drone position
* side position
* frontal position
* behind subject

Camera relationship:

* distance from subjects
* viewing direction
* spatial relationship between camera and action

Camera behavior:

* static
* slow push-in
* tracking
* handheld observation
* controlled pan
* crane movement

Lens behavior when important:

* wide lens for scale
* telephoto compression
* shallow depth of field
* deep focus

The camera setup must be physically achievable by a real documentary crew.

Use only one continuous camera setup.

Do not describe:

* subject appearance
* environment details
* chronological action

---

3. Action timeline extraction

Break the shot into chronological visible action phases that can occur naturally within approximately 5–8 seconds.

Each phase must describe what physically happens next.

Focus on:

* initial posture
* body orientation
* movement direction
* speed
* acceleration or deceleration
* approach or separation distance
* predator-prey relationship
* physical contact
* reaction after interaction
* interaction with terrain or objects

For predator-prey scenes always preserve:

* who is predator
* who is prey
* who initiates movement
* who escapes
* who pursues
* whether physical contact happens

Do not invent unrealistic behavior.

Avoid cinematic interpretation.

Describe observable physical events only.

Do not mention:

* camera
* grading
* cinematic mood
* music

---

4. Visible physical context

Describe only environmental elements physically visible and materially relevant to the shot.

Include when appropriate:

* terrain
* vegetation
* water
* snow
* mud
* rocks
* branches
* caves
* grassland
* weather
* lighting conditions
* obstacles
* ice
* exposed earth
* river channels

The environment must support the action.

Avoid generic descriptions.

Do not repeat:

* subject appearance
* camera instructions
* action timeline

---

5. Audio extraction

Identify natural sounds realistically present in the shot.

Include when appropriate:

* animal vocalizations
* footsteps
* breathing
* impacts
* water
* wind
* insects
* birds
* vegetation
* snow compression
* ice cracking
* tools contacting objects

Do not add:

* music
* narration
* emotional sound design

unless explicitly required by the script.

---

6. Negative failure conditions

Identify specific outcomes that would make the generated shot incorrect.

Focus on:

* wrong species relationship
* incorrect scale
* impossible movement
* incorrect anatomy
* impossible body posture
* unrealistic interaction
* impossible camera motion
* modern objects
* incorrect terrain
* visibly artificial CGI appearance

Use short failure descriptions.

---

7. Physical realism rules

All shots must follow real-world physics.

Avoid:

* impossible animal speeds
* impossible camera positions
* multiple cuts inside one shot
* teleporting subjects
* contradictory movement
* impossible simultaneous actions
* morphing environments
* animals changing identity
* unrealistic group behavior

IMPORTANT:

If the script contains a complex event, DO NOT choose only the single most important moment.

Instead, divide the complex event into multiple consecutive physically achievable shots, with each shot representing one useful continuous visual phase.

==================================================
DOCUMENTARY VISUAL PRIORITY
===========================

Prioritize:

1. Complete visual coverage of narration
2. Clear subject readability
3. Correct spatial relationship
4. Realistic movement
5. Scientific accuracy
6. Shot-scale variation
7. Cinematic composition

The output will be used directly for:

* Veo video generation
* wildlife documentary reconstruction
* CGI previsualization
* documentary shot planning

Produce a professional SHOT LIST rather than prose narration.

Do not intentionally reduce the shot count.

Do not summarize several visually distinct moments into one shot.

For approximately 10 minutes of narration, aim for roughly 70–80 independently generatable shots.

shots.cinematography: Extreme wide ground-level rear three-quarter view on a 28mm lens, camera several dozen meters behind the traveling group, with deep focus from the foreground ground to the distant horizon; a slow, steady forward track preserves the group’s scale against the open landscape.
action_timeline: The small human group begins clustered near the edge of the open plain, each person carrying folded hides or stone tools.
The lead travelers start forward, followed by the rest of the group in a loose line.
The group steadily increases its distance from the camera and continues across the open ground without any predator pursuit.
shots.context: Late Pleistocene central European cold steppe in summer, with sparse woodland patches, wind-bent grasses, crusted frozen ground, and shallow areas where the surface has thawed but the deeper soil remains frozen.
shots.audio: Cold wind across grass, measured footsteps on hard ground, hide bundles rubbing, and occasional stone-tool clacks.

shots.cinematography: Wide lateral tracking shot on a 35mm lens from waist height, keeping the entire traveling line in profile with the horizon visible behind them; movement remains parallel and smooth throughout the shot.
action_timeline: The group crosses from left to right in a loose traveling line across the grassland.
A person near the rear briefly slows as a hide bundle shifts, then resumes the group’s pace.
The travelers pass behind a low rise and continue toward the distant plain.
shots.context: Open cold-resistant grassland with shallow wind-scoured ridges, sparse sedges, and no enclosing forest; the terrain is broad enough for the group to remain visually separated.
shots.audio: Footsteps through dry grass, fabric and hide movement, wind, and subdued breathing.

shots.cinematography: Medium side-on observational shot on a 50mm lens, camera at chest height and positioned a few meters from the lead traveler; shallow background separation keeps the carried materials readable while retaining the walking posture.
action_timeline: The lead traveler walks steadily with a folded reindeer hide held against the torso.
A stone tool bundle shifts in the opposite hand as the person steps over uneven ground.
The traveler adjusts the hide against the shoulder without stopping.
shots.context: The immediate background is an open, wind-exposed steppe with low grasses and a pale, treeless horizon.
shots.audio: Leather and hide creaking, light tool contact, footfalls, and wind moving across the plain.

shots.cinematography: Close-up from slightly above hand level on an 85mm lens, locked to the traveler’s hands and waist while the person remains partially visible at the edge of frame; shallow depth of field isolates the hide and stone tools.
action_timeline: A hand tightens its grip around a folded hide bundle.
The other hand steadies several flint tools wrapped in leather or held together by cord.
The materials sway with the next steps and settle against the traveler’s body.
shots.context: Only the traveler’s hide clothing, folded hide, natural cord, and chipped stone implements are visible against a softly blurred cold landscape.
shots.audio: Hide rustle, cord tension, small stone impacts, and muffled footsteps.

shots.cinematography: Low ground-level close-up on a 70mm lens aimed at the lower legs and feet, with the camera stationary beside the route; the frame keeps the frozen soil, foot placement, and compression of the surface clearly readable.
action_timeline: One foot lands on a hard crust of soil and compresses a thin layer of frost.
The second foot steps forward across a shallow crack without sinking deeply.
The departing heel leaves a sharp impression in the frozen surface.
shots.context: Hard permafrost ground with a thin thawed skin, scattered dry grass stems, small stones, and shallow fissures from seasonal freezing.
shots.audio: Sharp foot crunches, small grit movements, and wind close to the ground.

shots.cinematography: Macro ground-level shot on a 100mm lens, static and focused on a narrow patch where the surface layer has thawed above visibly darker frozen soil; deep enough focus keeps the boundary between layers clear.
action_timeline: A small thread of meltwater moves across the thawed surface.
The water stops at a frozen ridge and gathers in a shallow depression.
A nearby grass stem bends in the wind while the frozen layer remains immobile beneath it.
shots.context: Summer permafrost with a thin wet surface layer, embedded ice, dry grass roots, and compacted soil that has not thawed through.
shots.audio: Faint meltwater trickle, wind through short grass, and occasional tiny ice clicks.

shots.cinematography: Extreme wide static landscape shot on a 24mm lens from a low ridge, with the sparse tree line occupying the far middle ground and open grassland dominating the foreground; deep focus emphasizes the distribution of vegetation.
action_timeline: Wind moves across the open grass while the broken tree line remains widely spaced.
A few branches bend and recover in the gusts.
The landscape holds as an open plain with only scattered woodland islands.
shots.context: Cold late-glacial steppe with increasingly sparse boreal trees, low sedges, dry grasses, exposed soil, and no continuous forest canopy.
shots.audio: Persistent wind, dry grass hiss, and distant branch movement.

shots.cinematography: Medium telephoto landscape shot on a 100mm lens, camera level with the broken woodland edge and held completely static; compressed spacing makes the gaps between trees visually prominent.
action_timeline: Thin trunks and isolated tree clusters stand separated by broad open gaps.
Wind moves the upper branches while the grass below remains low and sparse.
A small patch of woodland recedes into the distance without closing into a dense forest.
shots.context: Cold northern woodland transition zone with widely spaced trees, exposed pale ground, and grassland extending between the stands.
shots.audio: Wind through branches, dry stems brushing together, and faint distant bird calls.

shots.cinematography: Extreme wide telephoto shot on a 200mm lens from a distant low ridge, holding the herd small against the horizon; a slow controlled pan follows the group as it changes direction.
action_timeline: The reindeer herd moves in a loose line across the open grassland.
Several lead animals slow and angle sharply to one side.
The remaining animals follow the new direction, compressing briefly before spreading out again.
shots.context: Open cold grassland bordered by a broken tree line, with shallow rises and windblown sedges providing a clear route across the plain.
shots.audio: Many light hoofbeats, snorts, low herd calls, and steady wind.

shots.cinematography: Medium lateral shot on a 70mm lens at shoulder height, positioned beside the herd’s route with enough space for the leading animals to turn within frame; the camera remains static.
action_timeline: The lead reindeer pass from left to right with heads forward.
One lead animal brakes, pivots its forequarters, and turns diagonally away.
Two following animals mirror the turn, causing the line behind them to redirect across the grass.
shots.context: Low wind-bent grassland with patches of exposed soil and no physical barrier forcing the movement.
shots.audio: Hooves striking dry ground, short snorts, antler movement, and grass brushing legs.

shots.cinematography: Wide side-rear shot on a 50mm lens from a low ridge, placing the human group in the foreground and the redirected reindeer herd far across the same plain; a slow pan preserves their separation.
action_timeline: The people pause briefly on the ridge and face toward the distant herd.
The herd continues along its new route across the background.
The humans remain still for a moment, then one person turns back toward the direction of travel.
shots.context: Broad open steppe with a clear spatial gap between the humans and herd, sparse trees on the horizon, and hard summer ground.
shots.audio: Distant reindeer calls, wind over the ridge, and quiet clothing movement.

shots.cinematography: Medium rear tracking shot on a 40mm lens, camera following at walking speed behind the group; the frame keeps their backs, carried materials, and the open route ahead visible.
action_timeline: The group turns away from the distant herd and resumes walking.

shots.audio: Repeated footfalls, wind gusts, hide movement, and faint stone-tool contact.

shots.cinematography: Extreme wide elevated landscape shot on a 24mm lens from a rocky rise, with the ice sheet filling the distant horizon and open steppe occupying the foreground; the camera remains static for scale.

shots.audio: Deep wind, distant ice groans, and dry grass movement.

shots.context: Cold transition zone where sparse grassland ends in snow and grounded ice, with no forest blocking the herd’s movement.
shots.audio: Hoofbeats, reindeer snorts, wind, and distant ice cracking.

shots.cinematography: Low wide profile shot on a 28mm lens, camera positioned near the boundary between exposed ground and the ice margin; the composition emphasizes the abrupt change from vegetation to ice.
action_timeline: Wind pushes loose snow along the lower ice edge.

shots.context: Sharp ice-to-tundra transition with low arctic plants, exposed gravel, frozen soil, and a broad white ice surface rising beyond.
shots.audio: Snow hiss, wind, distant ice creaks, and brittle plant movement.

shots.context: Open grassland sustained beside a massive ice sheet, with dry sedges, low ridges, and scattered snow patches.
shots.audio: Low mammoth rumbles, heavy footfalls, grass movement, and distant wind.

shots.cinematography: Macro-to-close ground-level shot on a 100mm lens, static on a small cluster of grasses and sedges against a shallow depth of field; only natural wind movement changes the frame.

shots.cinematography: Medium low-angle shot on a 50mm lens from beside a young tree stand, with the mammoth’s head and forequarters in profile; the camera stays static to show the physical contact clearly.
action_timeline: The mammoth reaches a young tree and presses its head and shoulder against the trunk.
The sapling bends and cracks near the base.
The mammoth steps through the broken branches, leaving an opening in the stand.
shots.context: Sparse young woodland at the edge of open steppe, with thin flexible trunks, low branches, frozen soil, and grasses beneath the trees.
shots.audio: Wood cracking, branches snapping, mammoth rumble, and heavy footfalls.

Following animals widen the route by stepping over broken branches.
The herd emerges into the open grassland, leaving bent and snapped vegetation behind.
shots.context: Mosaic landscape where sparse woodland transitions into steppe, with broken saplings, flattened grass, exposed soil, and a visible clearing through the trees.
shots.audio: Branches cracking underfoot, mammoth rumbles, grass movement, and wind through the remaining trees.

shots.cinematography: Wide solitary behavioral shot on a 70mm lens from a distant side position, keeping one rhinoceros centered against a broad empty grassland; a slow pan follows its steady crossing.
action_timeline: The solitary rhinoceros walks across the open plain without another rhinoceros nearby.
It pauses briefly to scent the wind, then resumes forward movement.
The animal continues toward a low ridge and remains separate from distant herbivore groups.
shots.context: Open cold grassland with dry sedges, shallow snow patches, low ridges, and wide empty space emphasizing solitary movement.
shots.audio: Heavy hoofbeats, deep breathing, occasional snort, and wind over grass.

shots.cinematography: Medium three-quarter head-and-shoulder shot on an 85mm lens at the animal’s shoulder height, camera fixed as the rhinoceros passes slowly through frame; the horn profile remains clear.
action_timeline: The rhinoceros lowers its head slightly while walking.
The long front horn passes in front of the shorter rear horn.
The animal lifts its head and continues forward with the heavy shoulders and low body visible.
shots.context: Windy cold steppe with muted snow, dry grass, and no nearby animals or obstacles; thick fur and low body proportions remain readable.
shots.audio: Rhino breathing, soft snorts, heavy steps, and grass brushing the legs.

shots.cinematography: Close side shot on a 100mm lens focused on the rhinoceros’s upper shoulder and back while it moves past; the camera remains fixed and uses shallow depth of field.
action_timeline: The rounded shoulder mass rises and falls with each step.

The shoulder and back pass out of frame, leaving the empty grassland behind.
shots.context: Cold open steppe with windblown fur, sparse grass, and a broad body silhouette adapted to severe seasonal conditions.
shots.audio: Heavy breathing, fur movement, footfalls, and wind.

shots.cinematography: Wide side-profile shot on a 50mm lens from a low ridge, framing a mature giant deer crossing the open steppe with the entire antler spread visible against the sky; a slow lateral pan follows its movement.

The animal continues toward a distant band of sparse woodland.
shots.context: Broad Eurasian cold grassland with low vegetation, open sightlines, and enough space for the antlers to remain unobstructed.
shots.audio: Measured hoofbeats, wind through grass, and faint branch movement in the distance.

shots.cinematography: Medium low-angle telephoto shot on an 85mm lens, camera positioned broadside to the male so the antlers span nearly the full width of frame; the shot remains static for scale.

shots.context: Open steppe with low grass, no dense trees, and a clean horizon that allows the unusually broad antlers to be compared with the body.
shots.audio: Hoof impacts, wind, faint antler creak, and grass movement.

shots.cinematography: Medium three-quarter shot on a 70mm lens at the edge of sparse expanding woodland, camera positioned ahead of the male deer and angled along the tree line; a slow pan follows its cautious turn.
action_timeline: The giant deer approaches a gap between young trees.
Its antlers pass close to thin branches as it turns its head to enter the opening.
The animal hesitates, angles its body around the densest stems, and continues through the sparse woodland edge.
shots.context: Early expanding woodland with thin trunks, open gaps, low branches, and enough clearance to show possible antler obstruction without trapping the animal.
shots.audio: Branches brushing antlers, hoofsteps on leaf litter and frozen soil, wind, and soft vegetation movement.

shots.cinematography: Wide telephoto shot on a 200mm lens from a distant low position, compressing a herbivore gathering in the middle distance while a cave lion appears at the edge of the grassland; the camera remains static and observational.
action_timeline: Giant deer and steppe bison move through the same open feeding area.

shots.context: Open Eurasian steppe with low grasses, shallow rises, sparse woodland far behind, and enough distance to preserve a clear predator-prey relationship.

CINEMATOGRAPHY:
Extreme wide ground-level rear three-quarter view on a 28mm lens, camera several dozen meters behind the traveling group, with deep focus from the foreground ground to the distant horizon; a slow, steady forward track preserves the group’s scale against the open landscape.

SUBJECTS:
1. Homo sapiens — Pleistocene hunter-gatherer
ID: homo_sapiens_—_pleistocene_hunter-gatherer
Appearance: Anatomically modern human with an upright bipedal body, relatively long limbs, a comparatively narrow trunk, high rounded cranial vault, near-vertical forehead, reduced brow ridges, and a lightly projecting face. Skin, hair, and eye pigmentation varied among populations; there is no single universal Ice Age appearance. Upper Paleolithic people should look biologically modern, not apelike or cartoonishly primitive.
Real-world size: standing height 150-190 cm; mass 45-100 kg
Scale reference: Adult humans are small beside mammoths, rhinoceroses, and bison. Clothing, hides, and tools alter the silhouette but not the underlying biological proportions. Clovis-associated people are Homo sapiens, not a separate human species.
Motion reference: Efficient upright biped capable of walking, running, climbing, throwing, fine hand manipulation, endurance travel, and coordinated spear use.
Behavior reference: Lives in mobile cooperative groups; hunts, processes food, works hides, uses fire and lamps, creates symbolic markings, and follows seasonal animal migrations. Social organization and technology are important visual cues, but the people should not be depicted as uniformly muscular or culturally identical.

2. Paleolithic hide clothing and hide shelters
ID: paleolithic_hide_clothing_and_hide_shelters
Appearance: Fitted garments, wraps, blankets, and temporary tents made from sewn animal hides or skins, with visible seams, lacing, folds, fur direction, and layered insulation. Clothing should fit closely enough for movement and thermal protection. Do not use woven modern fabric, metal fasteners, fantasy fur armor, or a single universal costume.
Real-world size: mass 1-30 kg
Scale reference: Garments follow human body scale; hide tents or blankets can span several metres. Hide type, fur retention, cut, and decoration varied by region and period.
Motion reference: Flexible material that folds, stretches, flaps in wind, and moves with the wearer; tent hides can billow or sag over frames.
Behavior reference: Provides insulation, weather protection, bedding, and portable shelter. Hide preparation involves scraping, stretching, sewing, and repeated repair.

3. Paleolithic flint-and-bone tool assemblage
ID: paleolithic_flint-and-bone_tool_assemblage
Appearance: Collection of chipped flint spear points, long stone blades, scrapers, engraving tools, bone needles with pierced eyes, and spear throwers. Stone edges should be irregularly knapped and functional, while bone tools should show polished working surfaces and organic curvature. Do not use metal blades, modern machined symmetry, or fantasy weapons.
Real-world size: mass 0.05-5 kg
Scale reference: Most individual tools are hand-sized; spear shafts and spear throwers create longer silhouettes. The assemblage is small relative to the people and animals using it.
Motion reference: Stationary when stored; manipulated through cutting, scraping, piercing, engraving, throwing, and hafting.
Behavior reference: Represents technological planning, hide processing, hunting at distance, sewing, and bone or antler working. Tool form should vary by task rather than appearing as one standardized kit.

4. Mammoth-steppe or steppe-tundra ecosystem
ID: mammoth-steppe_or_steppe-tundra_ecosystem
Appearance: Cold, dry open grassland mosaic containing grasses, sedges, flowering forbs, dwarf shrubs, patches of bare soil, shallow snow, and occasional sparse trees or shrub thickets. It should look productive and biologically rich, not like a featureless white desert. The ecosystem supported dense herds of large grazers.
Scale reference: Landscape-scale biome extending across portions of Eurasia and North America. It was a variable mosaic rather than a uniform habitat with identical vegetation everywhere.
Motion reference: Vegetation moves with wind and seasonal growth; snow cover accumulates and thins; rivers and shallow channels may cross the open ground.
Behavior reference: Maintained partly by grazing, trampling, browsing, and nutrient return from megaherbivores. Loss of the large herds allowed shrubs, tundra, and forest to expand in many regions.

5. Pleistocene northern boreal forest and expanding woodland
ID: pleistocene_northern_boreal_forest_and_expanding_woodland
Appearance: Patchy woodland of conifers, birch, willow, and other cold-tolerant trees with shrubs, leaf litter, open glades, and shaded ground. During forest expansion it should often appear as a mosaic or parkland rather than an impenetrable modern forest. Do not use tropical rainforest structure for northern Europe or Siberia.
Real-world size: standing height 500-2500 cm
Scale reference: Individual trees may range from small shrubs to roughly 25 m, while the ecological entity is landscape-scale. Forest expansion fragmented the open steppe corridors used by large grazers.
Motion reference: Trees grow slowly, sway in wind, shed leaves or needles, and spread through seedling establishment and vegetative growth.
Behavior reference: Provides browse, shelter, and shade but reduces continuous open grazing habitat. Increasing woodland is a major visual contrast with the earlier mammoth-steppe landscape.

6. Pleistocene permafrost ground
ID: pleistocene_permafrost_ground
Appearance: Frozen mineral soil and sediment containing ice lenses and organic matter beneath a shallow seasonally thawed surface. The visible ground may be dry, cracked, gravelly, grass-covered, or snow-patched. It should not be confused with a solid glacier or permanent deep snowfield.
Scale reference: Permafrost is a subsurface condition extending across broad regions; the active thaw layer is much shallower than the frozen ground beneath it. Local thickness varies substantially.
Motion reference: Mostly static on human timescales, with seasonal thaw, cracking, subsidence, and slow release of trapped water and organic material.
Behavior reference: Supports tundra and steppe vegetation and preserves bones, tusks, hair, and other organic remains. Thawing can destabilize the surface and alter drainage.
